{{Short description|Number of independent rational basis points with infinite order}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''rank of an elliptic curve''' is the rational [[Mordell–Weil theorem|Mordell–Weil]] rank of an [[elliptic curve]] <math>E</math> defined over the field of [[rational number]]s or more generally a [[number field]] ''K''. [[Mordell's theorem]] (generalized to arbitrary number fields by [[André Weil]]) says the group of [[rational point]]s on an elliptic curve has a finite [[Generating set of a group|basis]]. This means that for any elliptic curve there is a finite subset of the rational points on the curve, from which all further rational points may be generated. If the number of rational points on a curve is [[Infinite set|infinite]] then some point in a finite basis must have infinite [[order (group theory)|order]]. The number of ''independent'' basis points with infinite order is the [[rank of an abelian group|rank]] of the curve. 

In mathematical terms the set of ''K''-rational points is denoted ''E(K)'' and Mordell's theorem can be stated as the existence of an isomorphism of [[abelian groups]]
: <math>E(K)\cong \mathbb{Z}^r\oplus E(K)_{\text{tors}},</math>
where <math>E(K)_{\text{tors}}</math> is the [[Torsion_conjecture|torsion group of ''E'']], for which comparatively much is known, and <math>r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}</math> is a nonnegative integer called the '''rank of <math>E</math> (over ''K'')'''.

The rank is related to several outstanding problems in [[number theory]], most notably the [[Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]]. There is currently no consensus among the experts on whether one should expect the ranks of elliptic curves over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> to be bounded or not. It has been shown that there exist curves with rank at least 31,<ref name="largest">
{{cite web|url=https://web.math.pmf.unizg.hr/~duje/tors/rankhist.html |title=History of elliptic curves rank records |last=Dujella |first=Andrej |authorlink=Andrej Dujella|publisher=University of Zagreb |access-date=2026-08-21 |quote=The following table contains some historical data on elliptic curve rank records.}}</ref> but it is widely believed that such curves are rare. Indeed, [[Dorian Goldfeld|Goldfeld]]<ref>D. Goldfeld, Conjectures on elliptic curves over quadratic fields, in Number Theory, Carbondale 1979 (Proc. Southern Illinois Conf., Southern Illinois Univ., Carbondale, Ill., 1979), Lecture Notes in Math. 751, Springer-Verlag, New York, 1979, pp. 108–118. {{MR|0564926}}. {{Zbl|0417.14031}}. {{doi|10.1007/BFb0062705}}.</ref> and later [[Nick Katz|Katz]]–[[Peter Sarnak|Sarnak]]<ref>N. M. Katz and P. Sarnak, Random Matrices, Frobenius Eigenvalues, and Monodromy, Amer. Math. Soc. Colloq. Publ. 45, Amer. Math. Soc., 1999. {{MR|1659828}}. {{Zbl|0958.11004}}.</ref> conjectured that in a suitable asymptotic sense (see [[#Heights|below]]), the rank of elliptic curves should be 1/2 on average. An even stronger conjecture is that half of all elliptic curves should have rank 0 (meaning that the infinite part of its Mordell–Weil group is trivial) and the other half should have rank 1; all remaining ranks consist of a total of 0% of all elliptic curves over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.

==Heights==

In order to obtain a reasonable notion of 'average', one must be able to count elliptic curves <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math> somehow. This requires the introduction of a [[height function]] on the set of rational elliptic curves. To define such a function, recall that a rational elliptic curve <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math> can be given in terms of a [[Weierstrass's elliptic functions|Weierstrass form]], that is, we can write

: <math>E: y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B</math>

for some integers <math> A, B</math>. Moreover, this model is unique if for any prime number <math>p</math> such that <math>p^4</math> divides <math>A</math>, we have <math>p^6 \nmid B</math>. We can then assume that <math>A,B</math> are integers that satisfy this property and define a height function on the set of elliptic curves <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math> by

: <math>H(E) = H(E(A,B)) = \max\{4|A|^3, 27B^2\}.</math>

It can then be shown that the number of elliptic curves <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math> with bounded height <math>H(E)</math> is finite.

==Average rank==

We denote by <math>r(E)</math> the Mordell–Weil rank of the elliptic curve <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math>. With the height function <math>H(E)</math> in hand, one can then define the "average rank" as a limit, provided that it exists:

: <math> \lim_{X \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sum_{H(E(A,B)) \leq X} r(E)}{\sum_{H(E(A,B)) \leq X} 1}. </math>

It is not known whether or not this limit exists. However, by replacing the limit with the [[limit superior]], one can obtain a well-defined quantity. Obtaining estimates for this quantity is therefore obtaining upper bounds for the size of the average rank of elliptic curves (provided that an average exists).

==Upper bounds for the average rank==

In the past two decades there has been some progress made towards the task of finding upper bounds for the average rank. A. Brumer <ref>A. Brumer, The average rank of elliptic curves. I, Invent. Math. 109 (1992), 445–472. {{MR|1176198}}. {{Zbl|0783.14019}}. {{doi|10.1007/BF01232033}}.</ref> showed that, conditioned on the [[Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] and the [[Generalized Riemann hypothesis]] that one can obtain an upper bound of <math>2.3</math> for the average rank. [[Roger Heath-Brown|Heath-Brown]] showed <ref>D. R. Heath-Brown, The average analytic rank of elliptic curves, Duke Math. J. 122 (2004), 591–623. {{MR|2057019}}. {{Zbl|1063.11013}}. {{doi|10.1215/S0012-7094-04-12235-3}}.</ref> that one can obtain an upper bound of <math> 2 </math>, still assuming the same two conjectures. Finally, Young showed <ref>M. P. Young, Low-lying zeros of families of elliptic curves, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 19 (2006), 205–250. {{MR|2169047}}. {{Zbl|1086.11032}}. {{doi|10.1090/S0894-0347-05-00503-5}}.</ref> that one can obtain a bound of <math>25/14 </math>, still assuming both conjectures.

[[Manjul Bhargava|Bhargava]] and [[Arul Shankar|Shankar]] showed that the average rank of elliptic curves is bounded above by <math>1.5</math> <ref name="Bhargava Shankar boundedness rank Annals">M. Bhargava and A. Shankar, Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves, Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), 191–242 {{doi|10.4007/annals.2015.181.1.3}}</ref> and <math> \frac{7}{6} </math> <ref>M. Bhargava and A. Shankar, Ternary cubic forms having bounded invariants, and the existence of a positive proportion of elliptic curves having rank 0, Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015), 587–621 {{doi|10.4007/annals.2015.181.2.4}}</ref> without assuming either the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture or the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This is achieved by computing the average size of the <math>2</math>-Selmer and <math>3</math>-[[Selmer group]]s of elliptic curves <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math> respectively.

===Bhargava and Shankar's approach===

[[Manjul Bhargava|Bhargava]] and [[Arul Shankar|Shankar's]] unconditional proof of the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves is obtained by using a certain exact sequence involving the Mordell-Weil group of an elliptic curve <math>E/\mathbb{Q}</math>. Denote by <math>E(\mathbb{Q})</math> the Mordell-Weil group of rational points on the elliptic curve <math>E</math>, <math>\operatorname{Sel}_p(E)</math> the <math>p</math>-Selmer group of <math>E</math>, and let  Ш<math>{}_E[p]</math> denote the <math>p</math>-part of the [[Tate–Shafarevich group]] of <math>E</math>. Then we have the following exact sequence

<math>0 \rightarrow E(\mathbb{Q})/p E(\mathbb{Q}) \rightarrow \operatorname{Sel}_p(E) \rightarrow</math> Ш <math>{}_E[p] \rightarrow 0. </math>

This shows that the ''rank'' of <math>\operatorname{Sel}_p(E) </math>, also called the <math>p</math>-Selmer rank of <math>E</math>, defined as the non-negative integer <math>s</math> such that <math> \# \operatorname{Sel}_p(E) = p^s</math>, is an upper bound for the Mordell-Weil rank <math>r</math> of <math>E(\mathbb{Q})</math>. Therefore, if one can compute or obtain an upper bound on <math>p</math>-Selmer rank of <math>E</math>, then one would be able to bound the Mordell-Weil rank on average as well.

In  ''Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves'',<ref name="Bhargava Shankar boundedness rank Annals"/> Bhargava and Shankar computed the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves on average. They did so by counting ''binary quartic forms'', using a method used by Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer in their original computation of the analytic rank of elliptic curves which led to their famous conjecture.

==Conjectures on the boundedness of ranks==

It is in general an open problem whether the rank of all elliptic curves over a fixed field ''K'' is bounded by a number <math>\tilde{B}_{K}</math> or not. This problem has a long history of opinions of experts in the field about it. Park et al. give an account.<ref name="Park"/>{{rp|p. 5ff}} A popular article can be found in Quanta magazine.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/without-a-proof-mathematicians-wonder-how-much-evidence-is-enough-20181031/|title=Without a Proof, Mathematicians Wonder How Much Evidence Is Enough|date=31 October 2018|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]|last=Hartnett|first=Kevin|accessdate=18 July 2019}}</ref> For technical reasons instead of <math>\tilde{B}_{K}</math> one considers <math>B_{K}</math> the (potentially infinite) bound on <math>\text{rk}(E(K))</math> of elliptic curves ''E'' defined over ''K'' that occurs for infinitely many different such ''E''. We have <math>B_K\leq\tilde{B}_{K}</math> and <math>(B_K<\infty)\Leftrightarrow(\tilde{B}_{K}<\infty)</math>.

===Elliptic curves over number fields ''K''===

According to Park et al. [[André_Néron|Néron]] in 1950 held the existence of an absolute bound <math>B_{\mathbb{Q}}</math> for the rank <math>r_E</math> probable. [[Taira_Honda|Honda]] in 1960 conjectured for a general [[abelian variety]] ''A'' defined over <math>K=\mathbb{Q}</math>, which in particular includes elliptic curves, the existence of a constant <math>c_A</math> such that <math>\text{rk}(A(K))\leq c_A[K:\mathbb{Q}]</math> - such a bound does not translate directly to some <math>\tilde{B}_{K}</math> or <math>B_{K}</math>, but confers a favorable attitude towards such bounds.

In 1966 [[J._W._S._Cassels|Cassels]], 1974 [[John_Tate_(mathematician)|Tate]] and 1982 [[Jean-François Mestre|Mestre]] expressed their disbelief in such a bound <math>B_{K}</math> in various generality regarding ''K''. This was the consensus among the leading experts up to the 2010s. However Mestre in 1982 proved unconditionally that for elliptic curves ''E'' over  <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> there is a bound <math>\text{rk}(E(\mathbb{Q}))\leq O(\log (N(E)))</math> in terms of the [[conductor of an elliptic curve]] <math>N(E)</math> which itself is unbounded for varying ''E''.

In 2016 Park et al. introduced a new random model drawing on analogies to the [[Cohen-Lenstra heuristics]] for [[Class number (number theory)|class groups]] of number fields and the [[Jonathan_Keating|Keating]]-[[Nina_Snaith|Snaith]] heuristics based on [[Random_matrix#Number_theory|random matrix theory for L-functions]]. Their model was geared along the known results on distribution of elliptic curves in low ranks and their Tate-Shafarevich groups. It predicts a conjectural bound <math>B_{\mathbb{Q}}\in\{20, 21\}</math>. The model makes further predictions on upper bounds which are consistent with all currently known lower bounds from example families of elliptic curves in special cases (such as restrictions on the type of torsion groups).

For ''K'' a general number field the same model would predict the same bound, which however cannot hold. Park et al. show the existence of number fields <math>K_n</math> of increasing degree <math>[K_n:\mathbb{Q}]=2^n</math> for every <math>n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}</math> such that there are infinitely many elliptic curves ''E'' defined over <math>K_n</math> (in fact those elliptic curves have [[Natural_density|positive density]]) with <math>\text{rk}(E(K_n))\geq 2^n =[K_n:\mathbb{Q}]</math>, therefore a uniform bound for all number fields is impossible. They attribute the failure of their model in this case to the existence of elliptic curves ''E'' over general number fields ''K'' which come from [[Fiber_product_of_schemes|base change]] of a proper subfield <math>K_0\subsetneq K</math>, which their model does not take into account. Instead of the family <math>\mathcal{E}_K</math> of all elliptic curves defined over ''K'' they suggest to consider only the family <math>\mathcal{E}^{\circ}_K\subset\mathcal{E}_K</math> of all such elliptic curves that do not come from base change of a proper subfield. The model then predicts that the analog bound <math>B^{\circ}_{K}\in\{20, 21\}</math> should hold, however Park et al. also show the existence of a number field ''K'' such that <math>B^{\circ}_{K}\geq 68.</math> While as of 2024 it cannot be ruled out that <math>B^{\circ}_{K}</math> and even <math>B_{K}</math> are finite for every number field ''K'' (Park et al. even state it is ''plausible'') it is not clear which modified heuristics would predict correct values, let alone which approach would prove such bounds.

As of 2024 there is no consensus among the experts if the rank of an elliptic curve should be expected to be bounded uniformly only in terms of its base number field or not.

===Elliptic curves over other fields===

Park et al. argue that their model (suitably modified) should not only apply to number fields, but to general [[global field|global fields]], in particular including when ''K'' is a [[Function field of an algebraic variety|function field]] over a [[finite field]]. They also point out<ref name="Park"/>{{rp|p. 35}} that function fields ''K'' are known to exist with <math>B_{K}=\infty</math>, but that <math>B^{\circ}_{K} < \infty</math> for all such ''K'' cannot be ruled out.

For the question of boundedness of ranks of elliptic curves over some field ''K'' to make sense, one needs a [[Mordell's theorem|Mordell-Weil-type theorem]] over that field that guarantees finite generation for the group ''K''-rational points. This holds much more generally than only for global fields, by a result of Néron this is true for all ''K'' finitely generated over their prime field.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/Kktrace.pdf
 |title=Chow's K/k-image and K/k-trace, and the Lang-Néron theorem |last=Conrad |first=Brian |website=Brian Conrad |publisher=Department of Mathematics Stanford University |access-date=2024-05-04}}</ref> 

This fails for [[local fields]] such as <math>K\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{Q}_p, \mathbb{F}_q((x))\}</math>, as the group of rational points is no longer finitely generated. In this case the rank will always be infinite. For local fields, the ''K''-rational points have other useful structures, for <math>K\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}</math> one can talk about dimensions as manifolds or algebraic varieties, for <math>K\in\{\mathbb{Q}_p, \mathbb{F}_q((x))\}</math> one has an infinite filtration where the successive quotients are finite groups of a well classified structure. But for general ''K'' there is no universal analog in place of the rank that is an interesting object of study.

==Largest known ranks==
A common conjecture is that there is no bound on the largest possible rank for an elliptic curve over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref name="Park"/>{{rp|5–6}} On the other hand, Jennifer Park and colleagues at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] have published a [[heuristic]] model that indicates that the ranks are bounded, and that there are only finitely many curves of rank greater than 21.<ref name="Park">{{Cite journal|url=https://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/124997|title=A heuristic for boundedness of ranks of elliptic curves|last1=Park|first1=Jennifer|last2=Poonen|first2=Bjorn|last3=Voight|first3=John|last4=Wood|first4=Melanie Matchett|date=May 2019|journal=Journal of the European Mathematical Society|volume=21|issue=9|pages=2859–2903|doi=10.4171/jems/893}}</ref>

In 2006, [[Noam Elkies]] discovered an elliptic curve with a rank of at least 28.<ref name="largest"/> It was shown<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klagsbrun |first1=Zev |last2=Sherman |first2=Travis |last3=Weigandt |first3=James |date=2019 |title=The Elkies curve has rank 28 subject only to GRH |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1090/mcom/3348 |journal=Math. Comp. |volume=88 |issue=316 |pages=837–846 |doi=10.1090/mcom/3348 |access-date=2024-05-04|arxiv=1606.07178 }}</ref> that under [[Generalized Riemann hypothesis|GRH]] it has exactly rank 28:
:''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''xy'' + ''y'' = ''x''<sup>3</sup> − ''x''<sup>2</sup> − {{gaps|20|067|762|415|575|526|585|033|208|209|338|542|750|930|230|312|178|956|502}}''x'' + {{gaps|34|481|611|795|030|556|467|032|985|690|390|720|374|855|944|359|319|180|361|266|008|296|291|939|448|732|243|429}}

Many other examples of (families of) elliptic curves over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> are known.<ref name="largest"/> In particular Elkies gave an infinite family of elliptic curves over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> each of rank at least 19.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;99f4e7cd.0605 | title=Z^28 in E(Q), etc.|date=3 May 2006 |first=Noam |last=Elkies |website=NMBRTHRY Archives}}</ref><ref name="Park"/>{{rp|p. 2864}}

In 2024, Elkies and Zev Klagsbrun discovered a curve with a rank of at least 29 (under the GRH, the rank is exactly 29):<ref name = "largest"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;b9d018b1.2409&S= |title=Z^29 in E(Q) |date=29 August 2024 |archive-date=18 September 2024 |first=Noam |last=Elkies |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240918230710/https://listserv.nodak.edu/cgi-bin/wa.exe?A2=NMBRTHRY;b9d018b1.2409&S= |url-status=live |website=NMBRTHRY Archives}}</ref>
:''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''xy'' = ''x''<sup>3</sup> − {{gaps|27|006|183|241|630|922|218|434|652|145|297|453|784|768|054|621|836|357|954|737|385}}''x'' + {{gaps|55|258|058|551|342|376|475|736|699|591|118|191|821|521|067|032|535|079|608|372|404|779|149|413|277|716|173|425|636|721|497}}.

In August 2026, two curves with a rank of at least 30 and 31, respectively, were simultaneously published on the Elliptic Curve Rank Leaderboard (the ranks are exactly 30 and 31, assuming both the GRH and [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture|BSD]]):<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.spektrum.de/news/claude-anthropic-ki-findet-elliptische-kurve-mit-rang-30-und-31/2341336|title=KI findet die bisher komplexeste Kurve|language=de|trans-title=AI discovers the most complex known curve|date=2026-08-25|access-date=2026-08-27|website=[[Spektrum der Wissenschaft]]|first=Manon|last=Bischoff}}</ref>
:''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''xy'' = ''x''<sup>3</sup> − {{gaps|201|769|035|260|418|549|083|594|900|060|734|240|952|308|696|994|802|735|114|305|555}}''x'' + {{gaps|1|151|107|939|141|058|565|733|479|426|024|323|225|135|665|982|951|300|586|808|823|640|527|729|578|307|228|357|301|072|889|377}} (rank ≥30).<ref name=":0">{{cite web |url=https://elliptic-rank.icarm.cloud/curve/273 |title=Z^30 in E(Q) |date=20 August 2026 }}</ref>
:''y''<sup>2</sup> + ''xy'' = ''x''<sup>3</sup> − {{gaps|1|284|727|764|113|567|728|281|797|636|015|784|768|866|707|681|415|849|262|157|224|232|063}}''x'' + {{gaps|560|368|321|454|261|339|256|859|338|901|915|312|332|769|858|684|945|406|858|043|869|199|456|710|681|989|058|863|306|170|127|006|181}} (rank ≥31).<ref name=":1">{{cite web |url=https://elliptic-rank.icarm.cloud/curve/302 |title=Z^31 in E(Q) |date=23 August 2026 }}</ref>
The two submissions later attributed the findings to Levent Alpöge, Ava Howell, and [[Artificial intelligence|AI]]-based [[chatbot]] [[Claude (AI)|Claude]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Alpöge, a researcher for Claude developer [[Anthropic]], had previously used the [[large language model]] to disprove the [[Jacobian conjecture]] by counterexample in July 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Claude Fable 5 and the Jacobian Conjecture, Explained |url=https://www.datacamp.com/blog/claude-fable-5-jacobian-conjecture |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=www.datacamp.com |language=en}}</ref>
